title: Tabernash Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Tabernash wells have a 250 ft median depth, 10 gpm median yield, and estimated finished costs of $22,200-$37,000.
h1: What Wells Are Like Around Tabernash
intro_html:
Buying land around Tabernash means dealing mainly with mountain bedrock, not a predictable shallow sand-and-gravel aquifer. The permitted-well record within 5 miles includes 3,593 wells, with 2,245 recorded as constructed. Among wells reporting measurements, the median depth is 250 feet and the median pump yield is 10.0 gallons per minute.

Those numbers are useful for early budgeting, but they are not a guarantee for a particular lot. Most permits name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer. Neighboring wells, access for a rig, septic layout, and the specific bedrock under the property can change the result.

sections.heading: Tabernash well depths: plan for mountain bedrock
sections.html:
The median permitted well depth near Tabernash is 250 feet. The middle half runs from 150 to 352 feet, meaning a bid based only on a shallow nearby well could be misleading. The 90th-percentile depth is 500 feet, and the deepest well in the record reaches 1,202 feet.

Depths are spread across the area: 14% are under 100 feet, 48% fall from 100 to 300 feet, 33% from 300 to 600 feet, and 6% are deeper than 600 feet. With 3,546 permits naming unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer conditions, fractures and local geology are major drivers. Ask a driller to price the expected depth range, casing, grout, and the possibility of drilling deeper if the first water-bearing fractures are inadequate.

sections.heading: Expected well yield near Tabernash
sections.html:
Reported pump yields have a 10.0 gallons-per-minute median, with the middle half between 7.0 and 12.0 gallons per minute. That is a workable planning range for many household systems, but it is a test result, not a promise that every lot will produce the same amount.

The local distribution is concentrated in the middle: 77% of reported wells produce from 5 to 15 gallons per minute. Another 11% report 1 to 5 gallons per minute, while 1% are under 1 gallon per minute and 11% are above 15 gallons per minute. Only 1,272 wells report a pump yield, so treat the result as a useful local guide rather than a complete survey. A low-yield well may still work with storage, but the system design and approval requirements need to be checked before closing.

sections.heading: Water levels and the local trend
sections.html:
The median static water level is 90 feet below ground surface, with the middle half between 60 and 100 feet. This is the depth to standing water after the well has recovered, not the total drilling depth and not necessarily the level while a pump is running.

The decade series does not show a continuing drop in the available records. Median measured water levels were 100 feet below surface in the 1990s, 100 feet in the 2000s, 90 feet in the 2010s, and 90 feet in the 2020s. Only 330 wells report a static water level, so use the pattern as background information. For a purchase, request the well’s construction and pump records, then compare its measured level and recovery behavior with nearby wells in Fraser, Granby, or Winter Park where relevant.

sections.heading: Who has drilled around Tabernash, and when
sections.html:
Permit activity spans several generations. The records show 7 permits from the 1950s, 67 from the 1960s, 530 from the 1970s, 450 from the 1980s, 933 from the 1990s, 696 from the 2000s, 301 from the 2010s, and 313 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2026. Older permits may describe systems that have been altered, abandoned, or replaced, so do not assume a permit alone proves current performance.

The most active drillers represented in these records are Mcpherson Drilling Company (Mcpherson, Benny Don) with 567 records, James Drilling (Keaton, Jordan K.) with 278, and Virginia Drilling Co. Inc. (Shuck, Otis C) with 188. These are record associations, not recommendations. Verify current licensing, insurance, availability, and the scope of a written bid.

sections.heading: What a new Tabernash well may cost
sections.html:
Fractured granite and gneiss make drilling slower and less predictable than drilling soft ground. The local cost model uses $65 to $100 per foot. At the 250-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $16,200 to $25,000.

A finished household system, including the pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work, is estimated at $22,200 to $37,000 at that median depth. A deeper hole, difficult access, extra casing or grout, and electrical or trenching conditions can move the price higher. When comparing bids, ask what footage is included, what happens if the hole is dry or low-yield, and whether pump installation and water testing are included. A driller should also explain how the final system will be sized for the well’s tested production.

sections.heading: Risks to check before building near Tabernash
sections.html:
Low yield is not the only concern. The record includes 1% of reported wells under 1 gallon per minute, and fractured-bedrock wells can vary sharply from one lot to the next. A dry hole or an inadequate fracture is a real project risk, so investigate nearby completions before buying and budget for an unfavorable result.

Water quality also deserves direct testing. Mapped sites within about 10 miles include 6 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 2 historic mine features, and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those locations do not prove contamination at a specific well, but they justify checking the property’s location and testing the existing water. Keep the well, septic system, and building areas coordinated. A Colorado DWR permit, exempt household-use rules, pumping limits, and any augmentation-plan requirements can affect what the well may legally serve.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a Tabernash lot
sections.html:
Before closing, obtain the DWR permit, well construction report, pump information, production test, static water level, and recent water-quality results. Compare those documents with wells close to the property rather than relying on the area median alone. The local record has 3,593 permits, but only 2,466 report a total depth, 1,272 report a pump yield, and 330 report a static water level.

For vacant land, make the well investigation part of feasibility work. Confirm rig access, likely drilling depth, power location, storage needs, septic setbacks, and a legal water-use plan. Domestic or household use accounts for 89% of the permits near Tabernash, while irrigation accounts for 1%. If the property is near Fraser, Granby, Winter Park, or another nearby community, do not assume its geology or water rights match the parcel you are evaluating.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Tabernash?
faq.a: The median permitted well depth within 5 miles of Tabernash is 250 feet. The middle half runs from 150 to 352 feet, while the 90th percentile is 500 feet. Some wells are much deeper: the deepest record reaches 1,202 feet. Mountain bedrock and local fractures can make one property substantially different from its neighbor.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Tabernash?
faq.a: The local model uses $65 to $100 per foot for fractured granite and gneiss. At the 250-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $16,200 to $25,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work is estimated at $22,200 to $37,000. Difficult access or extra depth can increase the bid.

faq.q: How much water does a well produce in Tabernash?
faq.a: Reported wells near Tabernash have a 10.0-gallon-per-minute median yield, with the middle half from 7.0 to 12.0 gallons per minute. Most reported wells, 77%, fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. The records include 1% under 1 gallon per minute, so require a property-specific production test before relying on the median.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Tabernash?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from well depth or yield alone. Mapped sites within about 10 miles include 6 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 2 historic mine features, and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These do not prove a particular well is contaminated. Obtain recent testing, review nearby site locations, and test for concerns appropriate to the property.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping near Tabernash?
faq.a: The available decade measurements do not show a continuing decline. Median static water levels were 100 feet below surface in the 1990s and 2000s, then 90 feet in the 2010s and 2020s. Only 330 wells report a static water level, so this is regional context rather than a guarantee for one parcel. Check the subject well’s own records.
